title: Volume of Pyramids, Cones, Spheres

findings.finding: The topic has no opening review, and the cone worked example uses the area of a circle directly as its base-area step.
findings.breakdown: The only new ideas are the factor 1/3 and the perpendicular height, but the cone example writes pi(5)^2 for A with no rehearsal. A student who cannot recall pi r^2 quickly stalls on the base area and cannot attend to the new formula.
findings.checked: The topic has no review block and no earlier topic. Pieces removed from the candidate: square and rectangle area (well below the level of the booklet); V = Ah for a prism (not a step in either worked example, which state V = 1/3 Ah); radius from a diameter (first needed in guided practice b, not in a worked example, and its answer shows r = 23/2).
findings.assumptions: Area of a circle is prior knowledge from the Area of Circles and Sectors booklet. A calculator is assumed.

repair.proposal: Add a short review before p3-definition-text. Find the area of each circle, to 2 d.p.: (1) radius 5 m [78.54 m^2]; (2) radius 8 m [201.06 m^2]; (3) radius 0.6 m [1.13 m^2]. (4) Write the formula for the area of a circle [A = pi r^2].

findings.doneWhen: Students have calculated the area of a circle from its radius immediately before the cone worked example.
findings.pipeline: claude: sonnet medium review, opus medium challenge (comparison run, 11 October 2026)

findings.finding: The first guided cone task introduces diameter-to-radius conversion without modelling that additional decision.
findings.breakdown: Copying the worked example's use of the labelled length would substitute 23 for r and produce four times the correct volume.
findings.checked: The cone example uses a labelled radius unchanged. No preceding teaching explains diameter conversion. The expected substitution inside the guided blank is student work, not a supplied explanation.
findings.assumptions: Radius and diameter are prior knowledge, but the first guided application changes the example's sequence of decisions. Calculator use does not resolve the geometric choice.

repair.proposal: Before the volume scaffold, add: 'The labelled 23 mm is the diameter. First find the radius: r = 23 ÷ 2 = ___ mm.'

findings.doneWhen: Students establish r = 11.5 mm before completing the volume substitution.

findings.finding: Extend the equal-height comparison by asking when a square-based pyramid and cone have equal volumes.
findings.breakdown: The task exposes equal base areas as the deciding condition.
findings.checked: Both base-area formulas and V = Ah/3 are used in the topic. Cancelling the common positive height gives s² = πr²; for positive lengths, s = √π r.
findings.assumptions: Both solids have the same positive perpendicular height, with s > 0 and r > 0. The squared relationship is a sufficient expected answer.

repair.proposal: After p6-q7-response, offer: 'A square-based pyramid has base side s and a cone has radius r. Their perpendicular heights are equal. What relationship between s and r makes their volumes equal? Explain using V = Ah/3.' Expected answer: s² = πr², equivalently s = √π r, because equal heights make equal volumes equivalent to equal base areas.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task asks for the condition and its explanation.

findings.finding: The pyramid example uses 11 mm without stating how it comes from the labelled 22 mm base side.
findings.breakdown: The horizontal leg is half a base side. Leaving that decision unwritten permits students to use the full side when forming the right triangle.
findings.checked: The diagram shows the construction but does not label 11 mm. Earlier pyramid teaching uses supplied perpendicular heights; p7-method supplies Pythagoras but does not explain this horizontal length.
findings.assumptions: Students know ordinary Pythagoras and are learning how to identify its lengths within a pyramid.

repair.proposal: Before the height calculation, add: 'The horizontal leg runs from the base centre to the midpoint of a side, so its length is 22 ÷ 2 = 11 mm.'

findings.doneWhen: The working explicitly connects the labelled base side to the horizontal leg.

findings.finding: The topic has no opening review, and both worked examples begin by finding a shorter side with Pythagoras, once with an exact surd result, which is not rehearsed here or in Part 1.
findings.breakdown: The first line of each example is h = sqrt(c^2 - b^2). Students who cannot quickly subtract the squares for a shorter side, or who round sqrt(2275) too early, stall on step 1 of every question, when the new content is finding the triangle inside the solid.
findings.checked: p7-method states the formula but does not practise it. No question in Part 1 uses Pythagoras. The proposed items were checked: 12, 8 and sqrt(65) = 8.1.
findings.assumptions: Pythagoras' Theorem is prior knowledge from its own booklet. A calculator is assumed.

repair.proposal: Add a short opening review. Find the length of the missing shorter side: (a) hypotenuse 13 cm, other side 5 cm [12 cm]; (b) hypotenuse 10 m, other side 6 m [8 m]; (c) hypotenuse 9 mm, other side 4 mm, give the exact answer and then 1 d.p. [sqrt(65) mm, 8.1 mm].

findings.doneWhen: Students have found a shorter side with Pythagoras, including one surd result, before the first worked example.
findings.pipeline: claude: sonnet medium review, opus medium challenge (comparison run, 11 October 2026)

findings.finding: Compare equal numerical face slant heights and sloping edge lengths to consolidate the distinction between their right triangles.
findings.breakdown: Equal sloping lengths do not imply equal perpendicular heights or volumes.
findings.checked: The worked pyramid models face slant height; p9-q2 supplies the diagonal hint for a sloping edge. For the proposed solids, h_A = √525 and h_B = √425, giving volumes 3055.1 cm³ and 2748.7 cm³ respectively.
findings.assumptions: Both are right square pyramids with positive dimensions. A calculator is assumed.

repair.proposal: After p9-q2-response, offer: 'Two right square pyramids have base sides 20 cm. Pyramid A has face slant height 25 cm; pyramid B has sloping edge length 25 cm. Predict which has greater volume, then calculate both volumes to 1 d.p. Explain using the horizontal legs of the right triangles.' Expected answer: A is larger; its horizontal leg is 10 cm, whereas B's is 10√2 cm. Their volumes are 3055.1 cm³ and 2748.7 cm³.

findings.doneWhen: The optional comparison explicitly distinguishes face slant height from sloping edge length.

findings.finding: The hemisphere example is drawn with a 3.5 m diameter but its working goes straight to 1.75^3, so the diameter-to-radius step is never shown in this topic.
findings.breakdown: This is the only decision in the two examples beyond substitution. Guided practice a then gives a 124 mm diameter with blanks that expect 62^3. A student who substitutes the labelled length gets a volume 8 times too large, and the only written model of r = d / 2 is in the hidden answer.
findings.checked: p10-formula-comparison marks a radius in both figures. An opening review is not needed: halving a diameter was practised in Part 1 (guided practice b, Questions 4, 6 and 7) and in the exercise just before (p8-q1-b and p8-q1-e), so the candidate's claim that the previous topic does not use it is wrong. One shown line is the smaller repair.

repair.proposal: Add a first line to the hemisphere example's working: r = 3.5 / 2 = 1.75 m.

findings.doneWhen: The hemisphere example shows the diameter-to-radius step as its own line before the substitution.
findings.pipeline: claude: sonnet medium review, opus medium challenge (comparison run, 11 October 2026)

findings.finding: Generalise the melting-spheres task to explain how the resulting radius depends on the number of identical spheres.
findings.breakdown: Conservation of volume explains why radii cannot simply be added.
findings.checked: The topic supplies the sphere formula, and p14-q14 already requires conserving volume and recovering a radius. Equating volumes gives R³ = nr³, hence R = r∛n; R = 2r requires n = 8.
findings.assumptions: n is a positive integer, r > 0, and melting conserves volume. Cube-root calculation is already required by the referenced practice.

repair.proposal: After p14-q14-root, offer: 'n identical metal spheres, each of radius r, are melted into one sphere of radius R. Express R in terms of n and r. How many original spheres are needed to double the radius? Explain.' Expected answer: (4/3)πR³ = n(4/3)πr³, so R = r∛n; eight spheres double the radius.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task connects conservation of volume to the cube-root relationship.

findings.finding: The topic has no opening review, and its first example uses V = Ah for a prism, a formula the booklet never states or practises; guided practice a then needs it for a cylinder.
findings.breakdown: After three topics of V = 1/3 Ah and the sphere formulas, the example writes V_2 = Ah = (4 x 7) x 3 with no rehearsal. Students who cannot recall the prism and cylinder formula, or who apply 1/3 to it out of habit, fail on the second component of the first composite solid.
findings.checked: No teaching block in any earlier topic states V = Ah for a prism or cylinder; it appears only inside spheres Question 15. Pieces removed from the candidate: V = 1/3 Ah and the hemisphere formula (taught in this booklet and practised in the exercise just before, including Question 6), and the shared radius (incidental).
findings.assumptions: Volume of prisms and cylinders is Stage 4 knowledge from the Volume booklets.

repair.proposal: Add a short review before the Key Ideas. (1) Write the formula for the volume of a prism or cylinder [V = Ah]. (2) A rectangular prism has base 3 m by 5 m and height 2 m. Find its volume [30 m^3]. (3) A cylinder has radius 4 cm and height 5 cm. Find its base area and then its volume, as multiples of pi [16 pi cm^2; 80 pi cm^3].

findings.doneWhen: Students have used V = Ah for a prism and a cylinder before example 1.
findings.pipeline: claude: sonnet medium review, opus medium challenge (comparison run, 11 October 2026)

findings.finding: Generalise the fitted-sphere cylinder to explain why the occupied volume fraction remains constant for a vertical stack.
findings.breakdown: The total sphere volume and cylinder height increase by the same factor.
findings.checked: The sphere formula and cylinder volume are available by this topic. A snug cylinder containing n spheres has radius r and height 2nr. Its volume is 2nπr³, while the spheres occupy 4nπr³/3, giving a fraction of 2/3.
findings.assumptions: n is a positive integer and r > 0. The cylinder fits snugly around the stack, touching the outermost spheres at its top and bottom.

repair.proposal: After p21-q11-root, offer: 'A cylinder fits snugly around n identical spheres stacked vertically, each of radius r. Neighbouring spheres touch, and the top and bottom spheres touch the cylinder's ends. What fraction of the cylinder's volume do the spheres occupy? Explain why it does not depend on n or r.' Expected answer: cylinder height 2nr; occupied fraction (4nπr³/3)/(2nπr³) = 2/3.

findings.doneWhen: The optional task specifies the snug fit and asks students to explain the invariant fraction.

findings.finding: The sphere and hemisphere examples use cubing without an opening review rehearsing the meaning and evaluation of a cube.
findings.breakdown: Both substitutions require interpreting r³ correctly. Confusing cubing with multiplying by three changes the central radius calculation in both examples.
findings.checked: Complete preceding teaching uses squares in circle area and Pythagoras but contains no cube calculation. The supplied immediately preceding exercise also uses squares and square roots. Cubing is used directly in both p10 worked examples.
findings.assumptions: Index notation is prior knowledge taught separately in the course. Calculator use is assumed for decimal cubes and volume calculations.

repair.proposal: Before p10-definition, ask: (1) Write 4³ as a multiplication and evaluate it. (2) Calculate 1.5³. (3) Calculate 7³. Answers: 4×4×4=64; 3.375; 343. Keep this review to prior index knowledge; do not include the new sphere-volume formula.

findings.doneWhen: Students rehearse interpreting and evaluating integer and decimal cubes before the examples.

findings.finding: The pyramid example goes straight to 61^2 - 11^2: nothing says that the face height is the hypotenuse or that the other side is half the 22 mm base side, so the 11 is unexplained.
findings.breakdown: The diagram shows 22 mm and 61 mm only. The decision the topic teaches, which right-angled triangle to use and what its sides are, is never written down. In guided practice a the student must halve 20 unaided and may calculate 26^2 - 20^2. The same choice recurs in 1d, 1f and Question 3.
findings.checked: p7-method gives only a = sqrt(c^2 - b^2). The cone example has the radius as a leg already, so it does not show the halving. Part 1 defines the perpendicular height only. The halving appears only in the hidden answer to guided practice a.
findings.assumptions: The finding stands whether or not students have met slant height in the surface area booklet, because the example still hides the step.

repair.proposal: Add a first line to the pyramid example's working: 22 / 2 = 11 mm. Add to Key Ideas step 1: c is the slant length on the diagram; b is half the base side for a pyramid's face height, or the radius for a cone.

findings.doneWhen: The pyramid example shows where 11 comes from, and the Key Ideas name the hypotenuse and the other side for both solids.
findings.pipeline: claude: sonnet medium review, opus medium challenge (comparison run, 11 October 2026)

findings.finding: The first pyramid in Question 1 (part c) has a rectangular base with two different face heights and labelled half-lengths, while the examples and guided practice used a square base with one face height and the full side.
findings.breakdown: Three things change together: the student must pair each face height with the correct half-length (68 with 32, 61 with 11; pairing 68 with 11 gives a wrong height), the halves are given so the base area needs 22 x 64 recovered from them, and the base is no longer square. Part d, a square base with one face height, differs from guided practice a only in its values and is the bridge.
findings.checked: p7-example-pyramid-node and p7-guided-a-node (square bases, one face height, full side given); p8-q1-a and p8-q1-b are cones; p8-q1-d.
findings.assumptions: The diagram for 1c was read from its description only.

repair.proposal: Swap parts c and d so that Question 1 runs: cone, cone, square pyramid, rectangular pyramid, cone, rectangular pyramid.

findings.doneWhen: The first pyramid in Question 1 differs from the guided-practice pyramid only in its values.
findings.pipeline: claude: sonnet medium review, opus medium challenge (comparison run, 11 October 2026)

findings.finding: The hint in Question 2 tells students to use the diagonal of the base, but the right-angled triangle uses half the diagonal.
findings.breakdown: Question 2 is a fair closing challenge, but its hint is the only support for a triangle no earlier question uses. Followed literally it gives h^2 = 25^2 - (20 sqrt 2)^2 = 625 - 800, a negative number. The correct working is h^2 = 625 - 200 = 425, h = 20.62 cm, V = 2748.7 cm^3. The hint also uses the undefined term edge height.
findings.checked: p7-method, both worked examples, the guided practice and p8-q1 all use a face height or cone slant height with a one-step leg. Nothing uses a sloping edge or the base diagonal. The mathematics was reworked and agrees with the printed answer.
findings.assumptions: The challenge itself is kept; only the hint is changed.

repair.proposal: Replace the hint with: (Hint: 25 cm is a sloping edge. Its right-angled triangle uses half the diagonal of the base, so find the diagonal first.)

findings.doneWhen: The hint names half the diagonal, so following it cannot give a negative number under the square root.
findings.pipeline: claude: sonnet medium review, opus medium challenge (comparison run, 11 October 2026)

findings.finding: Question 5 asks for a radius from a given volume, and Questions 11, 12 and 14 depend on the same reversal, but nothing in the booklet models solving a volume formula for a dimension.
findings.breakdown: Every example, guided question and practice question before Question 5 substitutes forwards. To find r students must isolate r^3 (multiply by 3, divide by 4 pi) and take a cube root. Likely errors are taking a square root, not undoing the 4/3 or pi, and dividing by 4/3 incorrectly.
findings.checked: p10-examples, p10-guided-block, p11-q1 to p11-q3 and p12-q4 are forward substitution only, as are all the worked examples and guided practice of both pyramid and cone topics. Proposed working checked: r^3 = 45 / (4 pi) = 3.581, r = 1.53 cm.
findings.assumptions: The course teaches ax^3 = k and rearranging formulas in other booklets, but their order relative to this one is unknown (see the context question). If students have just done them, the cue below is still enough. A calculator with a cube root key is assumed.

repair.proposal: Show the working for 5a as a model: V = 4/3 pi r^3; 15 = 4/3 pi r^3; r^3 = (15 x 3) / (4 pi); r = cube root of 3.581... = 1.53 cm. Leave 5b and 5c unscaffolded.

findings.doneWhen: One worked model of isolating r^3 and taking a cube root appears before students do 5b, 5c and Questions 11, 12 and 14.
findings.pipeline: claude: sonnet medium review, opus medium challenge (comparison run, 11 October 2026)

findings.finding: Example 2 writes r = 7 - 5 = 2 cm without saying that the height of a hemisphere equals its radius or that the cone shares that radius.
findings.breakdown: The student must see that the total height 7 cm is the cone height plus the hemisphere height, that the hemisphere height is r, and that the cone's base has the same r. None of this is stated, so the subtraction looks arbitrary and students may use 5 cm or 7 cm as the radius. The same inference returns in Questions 2c and 8.
findings.checked: p10-formula-comparison, p10-guided-block and p16-key-ideas-block: no block states the height of a hemisphere. Guided practice a gives the diameter directly, so it does not practise the inference.

repair.proposal: Replace the line with: The height of a hemisphere equals its radius, so r = 7 - 5 = 2 cm. The cone has the same radius.

findings.doneWhen: The example says why the radius is the total height minus the cone height, and that both parts share it.
findings.pipeline: claude: sonnet medium review, opus medium challenge (comparison run, 11 October 2026)

findings.finding: Describe one square pyramid three ways, by perpendicular height, face height and sloping edge, so students see three different lengths of one solid.
findings.breakdown: Each description needs a different right-angled triangle and all give the same volume, which prepares the sloping edge in Question 2.
findings.checked: Side 10: h = 12 gives V = 400; face height 13 gives sqrt(169 - 25) = 12; edge sqrt(194) gives sqrt(194 - 50) = 12. Follow-up: base 16, face height 17 gives h = 15 and V = 1280. All correct.

repair.proposal: Each question describes a pyramid with a square base of side 10 cm. Predict: will the volumes be equal? Then solve. (1) Perpendicular height 12 cm [400 cm^3]. (2) Face height 13 cm [h = 12 cm, 400 cm^3]. (3) Sloping edge sqrt(194) cm [half diagonal squared = 50, h = 12 cm, 400 cm^3]. Then: a square pyramid with base 16 cm and face height 17 cm [h = 15 cm, 1280 cm^3]. Varies: which length is given. Same: the base and the solid. Placement: after Question 1, before Question 2.

findings.pipeline: claude: sonnet medium review, opus medium challenge (comparison run, 11 October 2026)

findings.finding: Keep one cylinder fixed and add or remove a hemisphere or cone, so students contrast adding with subtracting.
findings.breakdown: The Key Ideas say add or subtract, but both examples and the guided practice only add. The run sets the same two solids side by side as attached and as hollowed out.
findings.checked: Cylinder 144 pi; hemisphere 128 pi / 3; cone 48 pi. Results 560 pi / 3 = 586.43, 304 pi / 3 = 318.35, 192 pi = 603.19, 96 pi = 301.59. Follow-up 90 pi - 18 pi + 15 pi = 87 pi = 273.32. All correct.

repair.proposal: All parts use a cylinder of radius 4 cm and height 9 cm. Before calculating, say whether each solid will be larger or smaller than the plain cylinder. (1) A hemisphere of radius 4 cm is added to the top [586.43 cm^3]. (2) A hemispherical hollow of radius 4 cm is cut out of the top [318.35 cm^3]. (3) A cone of radius 4 cm and height 9 cm is added to the top [603.19 cm^3]. (4) A cone-shaped hollow of radius 4 cm and height 9 cm is cut out of the top [301.59 cm^3]. Then: a cylinder of radius 3 cm and height 10 cm has a hemispherical hollow cut out of one end and a cone of height 5 cm added to the other end [87 pi = 273.32 cm^3]. Varies: the second solid and whether it is added or removed. Same: the cylinder. Placement: after Question 6, before Question 7.

findings.pipeline: claude: sonnet medium review, opus medium challenge (comparison run, 11 October 2026)

contextQuestions.question: Before this booklet, have students learned to relate the radius and height of similar cones and recover a linear scale factor from a volume ratio using a cube root? The supplied teaching does not establish that preparation, and it determines whether p22-q13 requires an untaught method.

protectedGroups.observation: Students must distinguish a radius from either representation of a diameter before substituting.
protectedGroups.varies: The dimension is a centre-to-surface radius, an equatorial diameter or the sphere's full vertical height; numerical values also change.
protectedGroups.invariant: Sphere volume formula, centimetre units and one-decimal-place answers.

protectedGroups.observation: The mixed set requires selecting the volume formula for each taught solid.
protectedGroups.invariant: Find volume from sufficient given dimensions and round to one decimal place.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing orientation preserves the volume method, and a second hemispherical end adds another hemisphere rather than changing the cylinder calculation.
protectedGroups.varies: Orientation, scaffold and number of hemispherical ends.
protectedGroups.invariant: A cylinder joined to hemispherical components of the same radius.

protectedGroups.observation: The same fitted sphere occupies different fractions of different enclosing solids.
protectedGroups.varies: The enclosure changes from cube to cylinder.
protectedGroups.invariant: An exactly fitted sphere and a request for its volume as a percentage of the enclosure.
